question: The two World Area Forecast Centres (WAFCs) are:

options.text: Geneva (WMO) and Montreal (ICAO)
Paris (Météo-France) and Frankfurt (Deutscher Wetterdienst)
Tokyo (JMA) and Sydney (Bureau of Meteorology)
London (UK Met Office, Exeter) and Washington (NOAA)

explanation: The two centres produce global forecasts for aviation and back each other up, so either can meet the global requirement if the other fails.

question: The main forecast products of the WAFS for flight planning include:

options.text: METARs and TAFs for all the world's aerodromes
SIGWX charts and upper wind and temperature forecasts
Runway state reports and SNOWTAMs for major aerodromes
SIGMETs and AIRMETs for every flight information region

explanation: METARs, TAFs and SIGMETs are produced by national meteorological offices; the WAFCs produce the global upper-air forecasts.

question: High-level SIGWX charts cover the band:

options.text: FL250 to FL630
The surface to FL100
FL100 to FL250
FL450 to FL600

explanation: Medium-level SIGWX charts cover FL100 to FL250 (some regional charts FL100–FL450); low-level charts are produced nationally.

question: WAFS upper wind and temperature charts are provided for levels including:

options.text: Only the surface, for take-off and landing
Every 1000 ft from the surface up to about FL600, for all routes
FL100, FL180, FL240, FL300, FL340, FL390, FL450 and above
Only FL050 and FL100, for low-level flights

explanation: These levels correspond roughly to the standard pressure levels from 700 hPa up to about 100 hPa and above.

question: SIGWX and upper wind charts from the WAFS are:

options.text: Actual observations at the time shown
Valid from the time of issue until amended
Valid for the whole of a 24-hour period from issue
Fixed-time charts valid only at the time stated

explanation: For a flight between two chart times, the pilot must interpolate between successive charts.

question: WAFS forecast charts are normally issued:

options.text: Only when severe weather is expected
Every 6 hours, about 18–24 hours ahead of validity
Once a week, for the following seven days
Every 30 minutes, as new observations arrive at the centres

explanation: Charts valid at 00, 06, 12 and 18 UTC are produced well in advance for flight planning.

question: For a flight from 1000 to 1400 UTC, using WAFS charts valid at 0600, 1200 and 1800 UTC, the most appropriate chart for the middle of the flight is:

options.text: Any of them, since all three are valid for the whole day
The 1800 UTC chart only, as it is the most recent forecast
The 1200 UTC chart, interpolating with the others at either end
The 0600 UTC chart only, as it was issued before departure

explanation: Fixed-time charts are only exact at their validity time; the chart nearest the time in question is used and others are interpolated.

question: On a SIGWX chart, a scalloped line encloses:

options.text: An area of significant weather, such as CB, turbulence or icing
An area of clear air with no significant weather of any kind
The axis of a jet stream and its core height
An area where the tropopause height changes sharply

explanation: A box linked to the area gives the details, such as type and amount of CB and the levels affected.

question: On a SIGWX chart, a dashed line enclosing a numbered area typically marks:

options.text: A volcanic eruption, described at the side
A tropical revolving storm, named at the side
A frontal zone at the surface, described in the chart legend
An area of clear air turbulence, described in the legend

explanation: The numbered area is explained in a legend that gives the intensity and vertical extent of the CAT.

question: On a SIGWX chart, "ISOL EMBD CB" means:

options.text: Isolated cumulonimbus embedded in other cloud layers
Frequent cumulonimbus with little separation
Isolated cumulonimbus standing alone in clear air, easily seen
A line of cumulonimbus with squalls

explanation: Embedded CB are hidden within layer cloud and cannot be seen visually; radar is needed to avoid them.

question: On a SIGWX chart, the descriptor "OCNL CB" indicates cumulonimbus that are:

options.text: In a line with squalls
Individual, isolated
Well separated
With little or no separation

explanation: ISOL means individual cells; OCNL well separated; FRQ little or no separation; SQL a squall line.

question: On a SIGWX chart, "FRQ CB" indicates cumulonimbus with:

options.text: Only a single cell in the whole area
Little or no separation between the cells
Wide separation between the individual cells
No associated turbulence, icing or hail

explanation: Frequent CB give an area that is difficult or impossible to fly through without meeting a storm.

question: On a SIGWX chart, cumulonimbus areas imply, without being stated separately:

options.text: Thunderstorms, moderate or severe turbulence, icing and hail
Only rain, unless hail is stated in the legend
Only light turbulence, unless more is stated in the legend
Only icing, unless turbulence is stated in the legend

explanation: Any CB on a SIGWX chart is understood to bring the associated hazards of thunderstorms, turbulence, icing and possibly hail.

question: On a SIGWX chart, "XXX" as the base or top of a phenomenon means:

options.text: It lies exactly at FL100, the chart's base
It lies exactly at the tropopause
It extends below or above the vertical limits of the chart
It is unknown and has not been forecast by the centre

explanation: For example, turbulence with a top of 140 and a base of XXX on a FL100–FL450 chart extends from below FL100 up to FL140.

question: On a SIGWX chart, a jet stream is shown by:

options.text: A scalloped line enclosing the area of strongest winds
A thick line with arrowheads, barbs for speed and the core flight level
A dashed line enclosing a numbered area, which is explained in the legend
A shaded area with the speed written inside it

explanation: The jet axis is drawn where speed exceeds about 80 kt; barbs and a figure such as FL310 show the speed and core height.

question: On a SIGWX jet stream symbol, the group "FL250/370" beneath "FL310" means:

options.text: The tropopause lies at FL250 on one side and FL370 on the other
The jet speed ranges from 250 to 370 kt along its length
The jet is at FL250 at 0600 UTC and at FL370 at 1200 UTC
Core at FL310, with winds above 80 kt from FL250 to FL370

explanation: The vertical extent of the jet (where speed exceeds 80 kt) is given under the core level.

question: On a SIGWX chart, a figure such as "350" in a rectangular box shows:

options.text: A jet stream speed of 350 kt at that point
The freezing level at FL350 at that point
A cloud top of 3500 ft at that point
The tropopause height, FL350, at that point

explanation: Tropopause heights are shown in boxes. Boxes marked with H or L show local high and low points of the tropopause.

question: On wind barbs, a pennant (filled triangle), a full feather and a half feather represent:

options.text: 50 kt, 10 kt and 5 kt respectively
10 kt, 5 kt and 1 kt respectively
100 kt, 50 kt and 10 kt respectively
50 kt, 5 kt and 1 kt respectively

explanation: A barb with one pennant, two full feathers and a half feather is 75 kt.

question: A wind barb shows one pennant, one full feather and one half feather. The wind speed is:

options.text: 115 kt
56 kt
65 kt
70 kt

question: A wind barb shows two pennants and three full feathers. The wind speed is:

options.text: 53 kt
130 kt
230 kt
105 kt

question: On WAFS upper wind and temperature charts, temperatures are shown:

options.text: As positive unless preceded by the letter M
In degrees Fahrenheit, with a minus sign where needed
As negative unless preceded by a plus sign
In kelvin, so all values are positive

explanation: At these levels temperatures are almost always below zero, so the minus sign is omitted; a positive value carries a "+".

question: On a WAFS upper wind chart, winds are typically given at intervals of:

options.text: 30° of longitude
5° of latitude and longitude
Every 100 nm along air routes
1° of latitude

explanation: Values between grid points must be interpolated.

question: Wind charts drawn on a polar stereographic projection require care because:

options.text: The winds on these charts are always given in degrees magnetic, not true
The temperatures on these charts are given in Fahrenheit
The scale is the same everywhere, so distances are distorted
North changes direction across the chart, as the meridians converge

explanation: The local meridian must be used when estimating the direction of a wind arrow.

question: To find the average wind for a route from a wind chart, a pilot should:

options.text: Sample the wind at regular intervals along the route and average them
Use only the wind forecast at the destination at the arrival time
Use the strongest wind found anywhere on the route
Use the surface wind at the departure aerodrome

explanation: Sampling at regular intervals, for example every 10° of longitude, and averaging gives a representative mean wind.

question: Two sample winds on a route are 330/20 and 030/40. A sensible average is:
explanation: Averaging 330 and 030 arithmetically gives 180, which is the opposite direction. Measured across north, they average to 360, and the speeds to 30 kt.

question: Winds sampled along a route are 240/30, 260/40, 270/50 and 270/40. The average wind is approximately:
Temperatures sampled at FL340 along a route are −48, −50, −52 and −54°C. The mean temperature and ISA deviation at FL340 are approximately:

options.text: −48°C, about ISA +5
−51°C, about ISA −2
−51°C, about ISA +2
−54°C, about ISA −1

question: A typical TAS used when converting an average wind to a wind component for a subsonic jet at FL300–FL400 is about:

options.text: 480 kt
900 kt
120 kt
250 kt

explanation: A representative TAS is needed to calculate the headwind or tailwind component on the mean track.

question: Upper wind charts for FL340 correspond approximately to the pressure level:

options.text: 300 hPa
250 hPa
500 hPa
200 hPa

explanation: In the ISA the 250 hPa level is at about 34 000 ft.

question: SIGWX charts show surface fronts as:

options.text: Standard frontal symbols, with speed and direction of movement
Isotherms only, without any of the frontal symbols on the chart
Not at all, because fronts are surface features
Cold fronts only, as they carry the CB

explanation: Surface fronts and pressure centres are shown on SIGWX charts with arrows and speeds, because they control the weather aloft.

question: A SIGWX chart symbol of a triangle with a dot or "volcano" sign marks:

options.text: A radioactive release only; check the NOTAMs
An area of large hail; check the legend
A tropical revolving storm; check the cyclone advisory
A volcanic eruption; check SIGMETs, NOTAMs or ASHTAMs

explanation: The symbol shows the location of an eruption; the side of the chart gives its name, position and time, and pilots are referred to SIGMET and NOTAM information.

question: On a SIGWX chart, a symbol showing a spiral of cloud (a tropical cyclone sign) with a name indicates:

options.text: A dust storm, with its vertical extent
An area of mountain waves, with its extent and levels
A tropical revolving storm, with its position and name
A cold front, with its direction of movement

explanation: Tropical cyclones are marked with their own symbol and name because of their severe hazards.

question: Which hazard would NOT normally appear explicitly on a high-level SIGWX chart?

options.text: Areas of moderate or severe clear air turbulence
Areas of embedded cumulonimbus
Low-level radiation fog at an aerodrome
Jet streams and their core levels

explanation: High-level SIGWX charts show phenomena above FL250, plus CB that reach those levels. Fog is for TAFs, METARs and low-level charts.

question: On an upper wind chart, the shaft of the wind arrow points:

options.text: Towards the nearest high pressure
In the direction towards which the wind is blowing, with the feathers at the upwind end
In the direction from which the wind is blowing, with the feathers at the downwind end
Always towards true north

explanation: Feathers are on the end the wind comes from; by convention they lie on the side of low pressure (and low temperature) in the Northern Hemisphere.

question: A route crosses an area on a FL100–FL450 SIGWX chart marked "OCNL EMBD CB", with its top given as XXX. For a flight at FL350, this means:

options.text: CB with tops well below the aircraft, so that the route is entirely clear at FL350
Frequent CB, but only below FL100, so they can be ignored at FL350
No CB at FL350, because embedded CB never reach above FL250
Well-separated embedded CB with tops above FL450, reaching the cruise level

explanation: XXX for the top shows the CB extend above the chart's upper limit, so they reach the cruising level and must be avoided, using radar because they are embedded.

question: On a SIGWX chart a jet stream symbol shows "FL340" at its core and a double hatch mark across the axis. The hatch mark indicates:

options.text: A change of 20 kt in speed or 3000 ft in core level
A break in the tropopause beneath the jet
The point at which the jet stream ends altogether
An area of volcanic ash crossing the jet

explanation: Change bars mark where the speed changes by 20 kt or the core height changes by 3000 ft.

question: A medium-level SIGWX chart for FL100–FL250 would be most useful for:

options.text: Turboprop or short-haul flights cruising between FL100 and FL250
Ground operations at the aerodrome
Light aircraft flying below about 3000 ft
Long-haul jets cruising at around FL390 on the oceanic tracks

explanation: The chart covers the levels at which medium-altitude flights cruise, including icing and turbulence at those levels.

question: On a WAFS wind chart for FL300, a station shows the figure "50" next to the wind arrow without a sign. The temperature is:

options.text: 50 kt

explanation: Temperatures on upper-air charts are negative unless a plus sign is shown.

question: On a SIGWX chart covering FL100–FL450, an area of moderate icing has its top given as 150 and its base as XXX. This means:

options.text: No icing below FL150 at all
Moderate icing from FL150 upwards to the chart top
Moderate icing from below FL100 up to FL150
Moderate icing at exactly FL150 only

explanation: XXX for the base shows the phenomenon extends below the chart's lower limit, here FL100.

question: For flights above the tropopause on a SIGWX chart, a pilot should expect:

options.text: Continuous thunderstorms, as the air is unstable
Severe icing in all areas, because the air there is always very cold
Fog and low cloud, as the air is very humid
Mostly smooth air, though CB tops and CAT near jets may extend there

explanation: Above the tropopause the air is stable and dry; hazards are limited to overshooting CB tops and turbulence near jets.
